newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: WEEK AHEAD-Jobs data seen dominating week.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-Jobs data seen dominating week.

text.p: Jobs will dominate the week ahead, starting with the ANZ job advertisement series on Monday and building up to the June labour force report on Thursday.

The weak employment market has been one of the main reasons behind the four interest rates cuts seen since last July, and signs of weakness in Thursday's data will bolster expectations that a fifth is not to far away.
Employment is expected to rise by 42,500 in June -- a seemingly strong number but one that in fact just reverses the 40,300 fall seen in May.

"The bounce-back is expected to be mainly statistical -- after last month's sharp fall -- rather than representing an upward movement to a more robust rate of job growth," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economists said in a commentary.
Such a rise would mean employment had only grown by about 4,000 jobs a month over the first six months of the year, and so would not been seen as an argument against a rate cut.

Economists said it would take a jobs growth closer to 100,000 to put a serious dent in the rate cut case, while a number less than 40,000, or a second fall in employment, would see expectations rise sharply.
"If employment falls again we would take the probability of of a rate cut later this month from 40 percent to 90 percent," HSBC Markets chief economist John Edwards said.

The unemployment rate is expected to come in at 8.7 percent in June. If unemployment comes in as expected it means that over the 1996/97 fiscal year to June 30, unemployment will have been 8.6 percent of higher for 11 of the 12 months of the year.

However, series such as the ANZ job ads and job vacancy series from the Bureau of Statistics are suggesting some signs of improvement should be seen later this year. Against that, business surveys continue to show a pessimistic outlook for
employment.
Apart from employment data, there are some minor price indicators, and May housing finance data on Friday.
After a strong 12.2 percent rise in May, a pullback of near six percent is expected.
However, economists said that this fall should be concentrated in refinancing, with new lending expected to rise consistent with the gradual housing sector upturn.
AUSTRALIAN BONDS (Fri: 10 yr bond yield 6.79 pct, 3 yr 5.70 pct)

Bonds finished last week on a bullish note, and with the U.S. having been shut on Friday for Independence Day, there is nothing to stop them continuing that tone in the early part of the week, traders said.
With the data schedule in the U.S. fairly quiet, local factors are expected to dominate this week.

Bond futures rallied to fresh contract highs, and the 10-year bond yield fell to its lowest level since mid-February 1994, on Friday after Treasuries had rallied strongly and overseas buyers and then domestic institutions bought bonds,
Sentiment is underpinned by expectations of a rate cut, and the positive news from Moody's Investors Service that Australia's credit rating outlook was improving.
While on the surface the employment data would appear to be unfriendly, a weaker than expected rise would be positive for bonds, underpinning hopes of a near term rate cut.
The market could even absorb reasonably strong jobs growth if the U.S. tone remained bullish, although the short end is vulnerable to a pullback.

"Solid jobs growth would not be irrelevant to the longer end of the Australian curve, but so long as U.S. bonds remain well bid they should not be as concerned as the short end with signs of stronger domestic growth," COmmonwealth Bank economist Tim Moloney said.
If employment is weak, the curve is expected to be well bid in the first hour of trading on Friday ahead of the 9.30 a.m. (2330 GMT) announcement time of any Reserve Bank policy change.
Apart form the employment data, traders said a cut could happen either after the release of June quarter wages and inflation data later this month, or after the RBA board meeting on August 5.
FOREIGN EXCHANGE (Friday Sydney close US$0.7519/24)
The Australian dollar remains under pressure from the talk of a rate cut, unable to break too far above US$0.7500, with sellers appearing on moves towards US$0.7550.
The prospect of a rate cut has been the dominant force on the dollar recently, and this week's focus on the labour market data is likely to do little to change that, traders said,

The dollar is epxected to remain in its recent US$0.7470/7550 band, with talk of a strangle option above US$0.7570 and the rate cut talk limiting gains, but good buying interest below US$0.7500 providing a solid floor.
Part of the reason for that floor is the expectations that commodity prices will strengthen this year and that some signs of stronger growth in the domestic economy will appear later in 1997.
If the dollar can hold up fairly well under the current pressure, analysts said it had significant upside potential.

"Once the market comes to the conclusion that the Australian economy has truly turned, yield support for the Australian dollar will quickly return the Australian dollar to favour," ANZ Treasury economists said.
AUSTRALIAN STOCKS (Fri: All Ords 2,733.4, down -0.35 pct)
Local shares are seen entering a consolidative phase in the near term with plenty of talk about how a breather was due after a bullish three months.
While noting the general tone remained positive, broker Kevin Lourey of Peake Lands Kirwan said a break looked to be sooner rather than later.
"There has probably got to be a pause for a little while," he said.
Others agreed, pointing to increasing selling in recent days as investors took profits and took stock of the situation.
"There has definitely been a bit more selling come along in equities. Some investors have started to take profits and lighten their positions," said dealer Martin Angel of brokerage Eyres Reed.
Further volatility in gold stocks was also likely to temper enthusiasm, as would any retracement on Wall Street when it resumed after the July 4 weekend.

"I think a lot will stay out of the equities market for now and sit back and see what the U.S. market does. The golds and resources will become extremely volatile in the next couple of weeks depending on what comes out," Angel said.
Corporate news remains thin on the ground with the announcement of final offer price for the offering of ICI Australia shares next Saturday the only event of note.
In terms of economic data, June employment data on Thursday is the big number to look for.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
